etymology:v2.5:nice.definition: Pleasant, agreeable, or kind; formerly foolish
etymology:v2.5:nice.lore: Once, calling someone nice was closer to calling them an idiot than complimenting their manners. Latin nescius meant “not-knowing,” built from ne, “not,” and scire, “to know”—the same knowing family that eventually gave English science. Old French inherited nice, and by the late 13th century English speakers used it for people who were foolish, ignorant, or simply silly. Then the word wandered through “timid,” “fussy,” “dainty,” and “precise,” acquiring so many delicate meanings that Jane Austen joked in Northanger Abbey (1803) that nice “does for everything.” By 1830 it could describe a kind person, while today it is often a mild all-purpose compliment—an astonishing journey from “you don’t know much” to “that was nice.”
